image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Proportional symbol map / bubble map** over a **geographic base map** of the United States.

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses a **single map panel** (no faceting or small multiples).
- Uses **symbol sizing**: circles are scaled by magnitude.
- Includes **layering/overlay**:
  - rail lines as thin gray line features
  - county/state geography as the base map
  - orange circles on top for derailment counts
  - a highlighted region (Ohio and Pennsylvania area) with labels

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County location (geographic position) | Spatial/geographic | Position on map (longitude/latitude) of circles |
| Number of derailed train cars by county | Quantitative | Circle size/area |
| Rail line | Spatial/geographic | Gray line paths on map |
| State / region highlight (e.g., OHIO, PA) | Categorical/nominal | Highlighted filled area and text labels |
| Year range: 1975 to 2022 | Temporal | Shown in title as the time span of the aggregated data |

If I could give this graph a title it would be “what is going on with trains?”

comments.raw_comment: This graph showcases the amount of derailed train cars in the United States since 1975.  The main point that I notice is how there is a rather large amount of derailments.  Ohio and Pennsylvania are highlighted, most likely because they were most affected by the recent event.  However, there is quite a few in those states specifically.  A decent majority of the derailments occurred in the eastern part of the country, but that is most likely due to the amount of rail lines.  There is more train lines in the states on the east in comparison to some of the midwestern states such as Utah and Nevada.  I also noticed how some of the dots are much larger, which I am assuming signals a higher frequency of derailments.  I wonder why these have occurred so much over the past nearly 50 years.  Railroads have been around for well over 100 years, so it seems it would be more likely that our technology has advanced enough to fix this.  I also wonder if any plans have been put in place to address this.  This relates to me and my community because derailments can be extremely dangerous so it is essential to know this.  I would entitle this graph: "Frequency of Derailments."

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
Although I had seen that railway derails were common in the US, I had never heard of them happening in other states. One thing I notice is that the midwest as a whole has an unacceptably high amount of derailments, even though Pennsylvania and Ohio are highlighted due to recent accidents. I found that the center midwest and the majority of the US's eastern region have the most derailments. Throughout the Western States, there is a tiny, dispersed group of derailed trains.

What do you wonder?
Given that trains are one of the oldest modes of transportation, I wonder if they have been modernized with more modern equipment. Might the problem with the trains derailing be with the actual railway rails? Could the weight of the cars be the result of too many passengers utilizing the train? Why is the Midwest the region with the highest concentration compared to the east and west coasts of the US? In the Midwest, where there are a lot of train derailments, how can people still use trains as a mode of transportation?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This is relevant to me and my neighborhood because of the train station in my town, which some people use to travel to towns farther distant from us or to other nearby townships. Pennsylvania, which we share a border with, has seen more railroad problems than New Jersey recently.

What’s going on in this graph?
Is the Midwest on the wrong track?

This is likely due to more railroads there, but less maintenance on older rails could also play a role. One question that this graph does raise is the severity of the crashes. A container carrying water that falls of a stationary train will do way less damage than a train going at 100+ mph carrying a small lake's worth of hydrofluoric acid and uranium-235. This can affect everyone that lives near a railroad, as any train could derail at any time, and if it's carrying some particularly toxic chemicals, could trigger evacuations for that area. One title for this graph could be: "Getting Off Track: Train Derailments Happen More Often Than You Think."

In this map, I notice that some areas towards the left have minimal spotting throughout the states, but as you move further into the midwest you can see the biggest orange dot around the Illinois / Michigan area. Trains Gone Wild:
I notice that in the states with more railroad lines, more train derailments had taken place. For example, in Nevada, there are very few train lines, so you can see that there are less trail derailments. However, in Ohio and Pennsylvania, there are way more crossing and overlapping train lines and you can see there are more train derailments as well. I wonder why states aren't doing more to try to stop the train derailments and to find a solution considering this has been going on since 1975. This relates to my community because I live in Washington and on the western side, there has been more derailments than that on the eastern part of the state. Also, there are many railroad tracks near my city and within it as well. This graph is showing the number of train derailments from 1975 to 2022.

comments.raw_comment: We do indeed need to worry about train derailments especially for ones carrying potentially toxic chemicals.  The case in point is the recent derailment in Palestine, Ohio.  In a study of air by the Carnegie Mellon’s Wilton E. Scott Institute for Energy around the Palestine train derailment, one of the chemicals detected was acrolein (a lung irritate and a known carcinogen).  It was found to be several times higher than in the air than the levels in downtown Pittsburgh on the same day.  Acorlein is also a product of automobile exhaust and has long been considered a potential health hazard in traffic tunnels.  The acorlein half-time (the time for half of it to decay) is on the order of less than a day, but if the input rates exceeds this then it will build up in air.  Wind may help dissipate acorlein but they could simple transfer the problem to a different place.  Acorlein air measurements should be carried out in a routine way both at further derailment site and the surrounding area.
